NHS flu vaccine page confirms: pregnant women eligible at any stage, injected vaccines contain no live virus and cannot give flu, protects mother and baby. Content correct. Source line named a title/season string that is not the page title or review date; replaced with the page title and its actual review date. Live-nasal-spray exclusion in pregnancy is Green Book teaching, not on the NHS page (uncontroversial). Key (88) not shortest (E 79) nor longest (A 95). No live duplicate (only PAN333 care-home flu).

edits.why_correct: The injected flu vaccine used in the UK contains no live virus, so it cannot cause flu, and it is safe at any stage of pregnancy. Pregnancy raises the risk of serious complications from flu, and vaccination also protects the baby during the first months of life. Pregnant women are therefore offered it each season. Source: NHS.uk, Flu vaccine (page last reviewed 29 September 2026).

checked.issues: RCOG GTG 5 page: OHSS is a complication of ovarian stimulation with excessive response, self-limiting in most, severe cases need inpatient care; fourth edition, page last reviewed 14 April 2026. Clinical content and distractor rebuttals sound (thromboprophylaxis in severe OHSS is standard GTG 5 teaching). Fixes: source line gave an unverified publication year 2026, replaced with the verified edition and review date; difficulty Difficult -> Moderate (classic vignette). Key (33) not shortest (B 28) nor longest (D 54). No live OHSS item.

edits.why_correct: Excessive ovarian response to stimulation causes enlarged ovaries and a shift of fluid out of the circulation, producing ascites, haemoconcentration, reduced urine output and breathlessness. The timing after stimulated treatment and the bilateral findings point to ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome rather than a surgical or infective cause. Mild cases settle with supportive care, but severe cases need admission for fluid balance and thromboprophylaxis. Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 5, The Management of Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (fourth edition; page last reviewed 14 April 2026).

CKS Ovarian cancer (Last revised in May 2026) confirms ascites and/or pelvic mass needs suspected cancer pathway referral, no day count; mechanism is standard pathophysiology (peritoneal seeding, lymphatic obstruction) and the stem rules out each distractor, so the key is sound. Fixes: capitalised 'Last revised in May 2026' to match CKS wording exactly; thinking chain ended on referral rather than the keyed mechanism, now ends on the mechanism. Key (80) not shortest (B 72) nor longest (C/D 81). No live duplicate (PAQ902/PAAKT141/PMG092 test investigation).

edits.why_correct: Ovarian cancer spreads within the peritoneal cavity, and tumour deposits on the peritoneal surface increase capillary permeability and obstruct the lymphatics that normally drain fluid, producing malignant ascites. Normal liver tests, normal albumin and a normal echocardiogram argue against the common non-malignant causes. Ascites with a pelvic mass should prompt a suspected cancer pathway referral to gynaecological oncology. Source: NICE CKS, Ovarian cancer (Last revised in May 2026).
edits.thinking: Pelvic mass plus ascites plus bloating  ↓  Exclude liver, cardiac and renal causes with normal tests  ↓  Peritoneal tumour deposits  ↓  Increased fluid leak and blocked lymphatic drainage  ↓  Malignant ascites

Key matches; distractors all wrong. Only fix: capitalised 'Last revised' to match CKS text exactly. Key (66) not shortest (C 52) nor longest (E 71). No live duplicate (PAQ995, DS099, ID039 differ).

edits.why_correct: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy can cause fetal anaemia, hydrops fetalis and fetal loss, so a pregnant woman with significant contact should be investigated even if she is asymptomatic. Blood is tested as soon as possible after contact, arranged with the local virology service. Source: NICE CKS, Parvovirus B19 infection (Last revised in February 2022).
